title: Esophagus and Swallowing: Structure, Motility and Aspiration
goal: Select the study for the symptomatic phase of swallowing, distinguish structural obstruction from disordered transit, and report airway invasion and oesophageal red flags.

quiz.prompt: A patient coughs immediately when drinking after a stroke. Which examination most directly shows bolus timing and airway protection?
choices: Videofluoroscopic swallowing study
Routine contrast-enhanced neck CT
Non-contrast chest CT
Static coronal sinus MRI
quiz.answer: Videofluoroscopic swallowing study
quiz.explain: A dynamic swallow examination samples bolus transit and airway protection. Protocol selection follows the oropharyngeal symptom, with speech and language expertise supporting interpretation.

quiz.prompt: During fluoroscopy, contrast enters the laryngeal vestibule but stays above the vocal folds. Which observation belongs in the report?
choices: Aspiration below the glottis
Laryngeal penetration
A pharyngeal perforation
Normal oesophageal clearance
quiz.answer: Laryngeal penetration
quiz.explain: Penetration stays above the true vocal folds; aspiration passes below them. Report when it occurs, clearance, and response to the tested bolus consistency.

quiz.prompt: An oesophagram shows a dilated oesophagus and smooth distal tapering. What prevents an overconfident diagnosis of primary achalasia?
choices: Smooth tapering excludes every tumour
A dilated oesophagus proves reflux
Clinical and endoscopic assessment for an obstructing mimic
Oesophageal motility cannot be assessed radiologically
quiz.answer: Clinical and endoscopic assessment for an obstructing mimic
quiz.explain: An achalasia pattern is a functional description, not proof of its cause. A distal tumour can imitate it, especially with an atypical history.

quiz.prompt: A contrast-filled posterior pouch arises above the cricopharyngeus and retains material after swallowing. Which diagnosis fits the location?
choices: Sliding hiatus hernia
Epiphrenic diverticulum
Oesophageal varices
Zenker diverticulum
quiz.answer: Zenker diverticulum
quiz.explain: The pouch arises at the pharyngoesophageal junction. Record retained material and associated swallowing dysfunction, because size alone does not describe its functional effect.

quiz.prompt: Severe chest pain follows forceful vomiting, and CT shows paraoesophageal gas and fluid. Which interpretation takes priority?
choices: Possible oesophageal perforation requiring urgent communication
An uncomplicated distal oesophageal ring
Physiological oesophageal contraction
A benign motility finding requiring no correlation
quiz.answer: Possible oesophageal perforation requiring urgent communication
quiz.explain: Extraluminal findings in this setting raise concern for a leak. State its suspected level and mediastinal or pleural consequences, and communicate promptly.

quiz.prompt: A referral says only “dysphagia”. The patient describes difficulty initiating a swallow, whereas the clinic letter describes food sticking behind the sternum. Explain what you would clarify before selecting the examination.
quiz.answer: Clarify the symptom location and timing, the effect of liquids versus solids, coughing or choking, and progression or other concerning symptoms. Difficulty initiating a swallow raises an oropharyngeal question suitable for dynamic swallowing assessment; retrosternal sticking raises an oesophageal structural or transit question. The two may coexist, so the referral may require more than one focused assessment.
quiz.explain: A symptom label is not a complete imaging question. Resolving the phase of difficulty avoids a technically successful examination that cannot explain the complaint.

quiz.prompt: During a swallow study, material passes below the vocal folds without a cough. A draft report says “no aspiration because the patient did not cough”. Correct the reasoning and describe what to record.
quiz.answer: This is aspiration despite the absent cough. Record that airway entry was observed below the vocal folds, whether it occurred before, during or after the swallow, the tested consistency, and whether material cleared. Document the absent protective response and communicate the result to the swallowing team for the patient-specific plan.
quiz.explain: The observed route of the bolus establishes aspiration. A clinical reaction is an additional observation and must not replace the imaging evidence.

quiz.prompt: Two studies show the same small pharyngeal pouch. On the first it empties completely; on the second it retains material that later spills toward the airway. Explain why reporting only its size loses information.
quiz.answer: The dynamic behaviour has changed even if the measured size has not. Report retention, emptying and any subsequent airway invasion, together with the bolus conditions and study limitations. The pouch provides an anatomical finding; the observed sequence helps explain symptoms and informs the swallowing assessment.
quiz.explain: Functional imaging describes events over time. A static dimension cannot capture delayed spillage or the effect of a manoeuvre.

quiz.prompt: A smooth distal oesophageal narrowing and delayed emptying suggest achalasia, but the patient has rapidly progressive symptoms. Write a cautious conclusion and name the unresolved question.
quiz.answer: The examination demonstrates impaired oesophageal emptying with distal tapering, compatible with an achalasia pattern. The cause remains unresolved: an obstructing lesion or other secondary process must be considered in the clinical context. Correlate with endoscopic and physiological assessment rather than declaring primary achalasia from the shape alone.
quiz.explain: Imaging can identify a pattern while leaving its mechanism uncertain. Preserving that distinction prevents the pattern name from prematurely closing the work-up.

quiz.prompt: A patient stops an oesophagram after two small swallows because of discomfort. No abnormality appears in the recorded segment. How should the final report distinguish the observation from the conclusion?
quiz.answer: State which segments and swallowing phases were actually assessed, why the examination stopped, and that no abnormality was demonstrated within that limited assessment. Do not label the entire oesophagus or swallowing mechanism normal. Relate the limitation to the clinical question and propose further evaluation if the question remains unanswered.
quiz.explain: A negative observation is bounded by the examination performed. Explicit coverage prevents a limited test from being interpreted as a complete exclusion.

title: Anal Cancer: MRI Staging
goal: Map anal tumour extent, sphincter involvement and nodal stations, separate local staging from distant staging, and assess treatment response with its timing recorded.

quiz.prompt: An anal squamous carcinoma measures 3.4 cm in its longest plane, without adjacent-organ invasion. Which T category fits?
choices: T1
T2
T3
T4
quiz.answer: T2
quiz.explain: Anal T category depends principally on maximum dimension until adjacent-organ invasion establishes T4. Use the longest dimension across planes and state the staging edition.

quiz.prompt: A 4 cm anal tumour extends into the external sphincter without invading another organ. What should the report do?
choices: Call T4 solely because the external sphincter is involved
Omit the sphincter because it cannot affect planning
Describe sphincter involvement without automatically assigning T4
Replace the maximum dimension with wall thickness
quiz.answer: Describe sphincter involvement without automatically assigning T4
quiz.explain: Sphincter and pelvic-floor mapping informs treatment planning, but sphincter involvement by itself is not adjacent-organ invasion for anal T4 classification.

quiz.prompt: Suspicious inguinal nodes accompany an anal canal primary. Which statement is correct?
choices: They automatically represent distant metastases
Only their total number matters
They are irrelevant below the dentate line
Their station must be recorded as regional nodal disease
quiz.answer: Their station must be recorded as regional nodal disease
quiz.explain: Anal nodal staging depends on involved stations. Record side, compartment, size and morphology rather than importing the rectal-cancer node-count rule.

quiz.prompt: A pelvic MRI maps the anal tumour well, but the referral asks for complete staging. What remains necessary?
choices: Assessment for disease beyond the pelvic MRI coverage
No additional assessment because MRI excludes all metastases
Replacing MRI with a lumbar radiograph
Using tumour length to estimate lung involvement
quiz.answer: Assessment for disease beyond the pelvic MRI coverage
quiz.explain: Local MRI and distant staging answer different questions. Chest and abdominal assessment and, where indicated, metabolic imaging complement the local examination.

quiz.prompt: Soon after chemoradiotherapy, the tumour bed remains thickened but has decreased substantially. What is the most defensible report?
choices: Certain treatment failure from thickness alone
Describe interval change, diffusion findings and treatment interval
Complete response solely because the tumour is smaller
No response assessment until a new tumour appears
quiz.answer: Describe interval change, diffusion findings and treatment interval
quiz.explain: Early inflammatory change and fibrosis complicate interpretation. Integrate morphology, diffusion, comparison and clinical timing; persistent thickness alone does not establish viable tumour.

quiz.prompt: An anal tumour measures 1.8 cm axially, 3.1 cm sagittally and 5.6 cm coronally, without adjacent-organ invasion. Which measurement governs the size-based T category, and what category does it support?
quiz.answer: Use the longest reproducible tumour dimension across the available planes: 5.6 cm. This supports a size-based T3 category. Record the plane and all useful dimensions, and separately describe sphincter, pelvic-floor and adjacent-organ relationships rather than allowing an axial measurement alone to understate extent.
quiz.explain: The largest dimension may be craniocaudal. A reproducible measurement and anatomical description make the stage auditable.

quiz.prompt: A draft anal MRI report imports a rectal-cancer template and assigns the nodal category solely from the number of abnormal nodes. Explain how you would repair the report.
quiz.answer: Keep the observed nodes but reorganise them by anatomical station and side, including regional inguinal and pelvic stations and any nonregional nodes. Describe size and suspicious morphology, then use the anal-cancer staging system and named edition for the category. Do not substitute the rectal node-count rule.
quiz.explain: A reporting template carries assumptions from its disease. Reusing its layout is reasonable only after checking that its classification rules apply.

quiz.prompt: MRI shows an anal lesion extending from 2 to 6 o'clock through the internal and external sphincters. There is no adjacent-organ invasion. Which details should survive in the impression even though they do not automatically make this T4?
quiz.answer: Preserve the circumferential involvement, craniocaudal extent and which sphincter layers or pelvic-floor structures are involved. State any extension to perianal skin or rectum and the absence of demonstrated adjacent-organ invasion. Assign the T category from the appropriate size and organ-invasion criteria, independently of this anatomical map.
quiz.explain: The category compresses information. Treatment planning still needs the location and structural relationships that the category does not encode.

quiz.prompt: After treatment, an anal tumour bed is smaller and predominantly low signal on T2, but a focal area remains indeterminate on diffusion imaging. How would you describe response without forcing a binary result?
quiz.answer: Describe the interval reduction and fibrotic appearance, then localise and measure the remaining indeterminate focus. State the diffusion limitation or concern, treatment interval, and change in regional nodes. Give a calibrated assessment of possible residual disease and recommend correlation with the clinical response assessment rather than declaring either complete response or failure from one sequence.
quiz.explain: Response reporting should explain both the favourable change and the unresolved evidence. This is more useful than concealing uncertainty inside a category.

quiz.prompt: The pelvic MRI is degraded by motion and does not reliably separate tumour from the anterior adjacent organ. A previous report described a preserved plane. Explain how comparison should influence, but not override, the current conclusion.
quiz.answer: The prior examination supplies a baseline but cannot prove that the current plane remains intact. State that anterior organ involvement is indeterminate because of motion, describe any assessable interval change, and identify the unanswered staging question. Further targeted imaging or multidisciplinary correlation may be needed before treatment decisions depend on that boundary.
quiz.explain: Comparison cannot repair missing current information. Carrying forward a previously normal relationship as a present finding creates unsupported certainty.

title: Small Bowel Tumours and GI Foreign Bodies
goal: Recognise bowel-mass patterns, map obstruction and spread, and actively search for sharp foreign bodies when focal inflammation or an unexplained abscess is present.

quiz.prompt: CT shows an eccentric jejunal mass projecting mainly outside the bowel, with central necrosis. Which diagnosis belongs high in the differential?
choices: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour
Simple intraluminal lipoma
Uncomplicated diverticulosis
Physiological jejunal contraction
quiz.answer: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour
quiz.explain: An exophytic soft-tissue mass with necrosis suggests a mesenchymal tumour such as GIST. Describe its bowel attachment and complications; imaging does not supply histology.

quiz.prompt: A small enhancing ileal lesion accompanies a spiculated mesenteric mass that tethers adjacent loops. Which association is most useful?
choices: The mesenteric mass excludes a bowel primary
A small bowel neuroendocrine primary can produce a desmoplastic mesenteric mass
Every such appearance proves active Crohn disease
The lesion must be a benign lipoma
quiz.answer: A small bowel neuroendocrine primary can produce a desmoplastic mesenteric mass
quiz.explain: A small primary may be less conspicuous than its mesenteric manifestation. Examine adjacent bowel carefully and assess vessels, obstruction and metastatic disease.

quiz.prompt: An unexplained focal ileal inflammatory mass contains a thin linear hyperdensity extending through the wall. The patient recalls no ingestion. What is the next interpretive step?
choices: Discard the finding because the history is negative
Call it intravenous contrast without checking another plane
Trace it on multiplanar images as a possible perforating foreign body
Ignore it if there is no free intraperitoneal gas
quiz.answer: Trace it on multiplanar images as a possible perforating foreign body
quiz.explain: Patients may not recall ingestion, and a contained perforation may lack free gas. Define the object, bowel relationship, abscess and adjacent-organ involvement.

quiz.prompt: A bulky circumferential bowel lesion has a relatively expanded lumen rather than a tight obstructing stricture. Which statement is best?
choices: This proves the lesion is benign
Malignancy requires complete obstruction
This finding excludes lymphoma
The pattern can suggest lymphoma but still needs tissue diagnosis
quiz.answer: The pattern can suggest lymphoma but still needs tissue diagnosis
quiz.explain: Luminal behaviour helps prioritise the differential. It is not a reliable substitute for histology, and overlapping appearances occur among bowel malignancies.

quiz.prompt: A sharp object is found at the margin of a liver abscess next to an abnormal gastric antrum. What should the report connect?
choices: Possible migration from a gastrointestinal perforation into the abscess
A liver abscess cannot have an enteric source
The object is irrelevant after leaving the bowel
The object proves a primary liver tumour
quiz.answer: Possible migration from a gastrointestinal perforation into the abscess
quiz.explain: Map the potential route, remaining object and collection. This supplies an anatomical explanation for source control planning without assuming that antibiotics alone address the cause.

quiz.prompt: An enhancing bowel mass is visible, but the lumen is collapsed and it is unclear whether the lesion arises from bowel or adjacent mesentery. Outline a report that preserves the useful findings without inventing an origin.
quiz.answer: Give the location, dimensions, enhancement and relationship to the nearest bowel loops, vessels and mesentery. Describe obstruction, bleeding, perforation or metastases if present. State that the epicentre is uncertain because of limited luminal assessment, offer a focused differential, and identify what additional imaging or tissue assessment would resolve.
quiz.explain: An uncertain origin does not erase the demonstrable anatomy. Separate measured observations from the proposed diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: A patient has anaemia and a short irregular jejunal narrowing with upstream dilatation. A colleague labels it Crohn disease because the wall is thickened. What competing explanation and supporting observations should be considered?
quiz.answer: An obstructing neoplasm remains a competing explanation. Assess the length and symmetry of thickening, margins, enhancement, adjacent invasion, nodes and distant findings, and consider whether there are other segments supporting inflammatory disease. Report the obstructing lesion and differential rather than converting wall thickening into a definitive inflammatory diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Thickening is shared by several diseases. The distribution and consequences of the lesion should guide the differential and further investigation.

quiz.prompt: An abscess has recurred after drainage. Thin-section review reveals a linear object at its edge, but the initial report said there was no free gas. Explain why the earlier negative finding does not settle the current diagnosis.
quiz.answer: Absent free gas does not exclude a contained gastrointestinal perforation. Trace the object in multiple planes and describe its location, possible bowel entry site and relation to the collection or adjacent organs. Highlight the retained foreign body as a possible persistent source and communicate the finding to the treating team.
quiz.explain: A negative secondary sign cannot outweigh a directly visible potential cause. The report should make the object findable for the team planning source control.

quiz.prompt: CT shows a small ileal enhancing focus and a much larger mesenteric mass. How can the impression connect them while preserving diagnostic uncertainty?
quiz.answer: Describe both lesions and their anatomical relationship, noting that a small bowel primary with mesenteric involvement is a possibility. Include tethering, vascular relationships, obstruction and metastatic findings. A neuroendocrine tumour may be favoured by the pattern, but histological confirmation and the clinical work-up determine the final diagnosis.
quiz.explain: The largest abnormality need not be the primary lesion. Showing the possible relationship makes the differential clinically useful without claiming tissue certainty.

quiz.prompt: A large exophytic bowel lesion has a necrotic centre. The request asks whether it is a GIST. What can imaging contribute, and what should it leave unresolved?
quiz.answer: Imaging can establish the apparent bowel attachment, size, viable enhancing components, necrosis and local or distant extent. Describe complications and explain why a mesenchymal tumour such as GIST is considered. Imaging cannot by itself establish the histological subtype or biological risk classification; those require the appropriate tissue and clinical assessment.
quiz.explain: A useful tumour report maps extent and supports a differential. It should not substitute morphology for pathology.

title: Dynamic Pelvic Floor Imaging
goal: Acquire and interpret rest, squeeze, strain and evacuation imaging, report compartmental prolapse and evacuation, and distinguish rectocele, enterocele and intussusception.

quiz.prompt: An MR defecography study includes rest and strain images but no evacuation because the patient could not empty. What belongs in the conclusion?
choices: A definite normal functional study
A limitation that may conceal prolapse or intussusception
Proof that the patient has no symptoms
Automatic diagnosis of severe anismus
quiz.answer: A limitation that may conceal prolapse or intussusception
quiz.explain: Evacuation can reveal abnormalities absent on strain images. Document performance and its diagnostic consequence; an unsuccessful attempt alone does not establish a specific functional diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: An anterior rectal wall bulge fills during evacuation and retains gel after the rectum empties. What is the relevant description?
choices: Only the resting rectal diameter
An enterocele because it is anterior
A rectocele with size and retained contents documented
A normal study if the bulge is small on rest images
quiz.answer: A rectocele with size and retained contents documented
quiz.explain: A rectocele is a rectal-wall outpouching. Dynamic size and trapping help explain symptoms and are more informative than naming the finding alone.

quiz.prompt: Small bowel loops descend into the space between vagina and rectum during straining. Which term identifies the contents?
choices: Cystocele
Rectal intussusception
Urethral diverticulum
Enterocele
quiz.answer: Enterocele
quiz.explain: The herniating contents determine the name. Identify the compartment and bowel-containing sac, and distinguish it from an anterior bulge of the rectal wall.

quiz.prompt: Two serial MR reports use different reference lines for organ descent. What should be standardised before declaring interval worsening?
choices: Reference line, landmark, measurement direction and manoeuvre
Only the scanner vendor
Only the rectal filling volume
The patients' surname spelling
quiz.answer: Reference line, landmark, measurement direction and manoeuvre
quiz.explain: Measurements require a reproducible anatomical reference and comparable functional phase. The pubococcygeal line is commonly used, with distances measured perpendicular to it.

quiz.prompt: A patient with obstructed defecation has pelvic organ descent in more than one compartment. What is the most useful reporting approach?
choices: Describe only the compartment named in the referral
Report each compartment and the adequacy of evacuation
Assign surgery from the most dramatic still image
Ignore dynamic cine images after obtaining measurements
quiz.answer: Report each compartment and the adequacy of evacuation
quiz.explain: Pelvic-floor disorders often coexist. Combine compartmental anatomy with the dynamic sequence, rectal emptying and study limitations to support multidisciplinary interpretation.

quiz.prompt: A patient strains well but cannot evacuate rectal gel during MR defecography. The anterior compartment descends, while no intussusception is seen. Write the key limitation that should accompany the findings.
quiz.answer: Report the observed anterior descent during the achieved manoeuvre and document absent evacuation. State that posterior-compartment assessment, including exclusion of an evacuation-dependent intussusception, is limited. Do not equate failure to demonstrate a finding during an incomplete functional phase with proof of its absence.
quiz.explain: The completed manoeuvre defines the scope of a negative finding. Performance is part of the result, not merely a technical footnote.

quiz.prompt: The bladder base lies 12 mm above a named reference line at rest and 18 mm below it during strain. Explain the observed movement and the information needed to compare this with another study.
quiz.answer: The bladder base moves 30 mm downward between those phases. Record the reference line, the bladder landmark, perpendicular measurement convention and which manoeuvre produced the lower position. Comparison also needs similar effort and acquisition conditions; the arithmetic alone does not supply a clinical severity category.
quiz.explain: Signed positions and displacement answer different questions. Preserve the measurement method before inferring progression or severity.

quiz.prompt: A rectocele appears large during strain but empties completely. Another smaller rectocele traps gel. Why should the report describe both size and evacuation behaviour?
quiz.answer: Size maps the anatomical bulge, while retention describes its behaviour during the test. Record the maximum dimension, emptying or trapping, coexisting descent and whether the patient reproduced their usual difficulty. Neither size alone nor one evacuation attempt automatically proves that the rectocele causes all symptoms.
quiz.explain: The most conspicuous still image may not identify the principal functional problem. Anatomy and observed function should be reported together.

quiz.prompt: A study shows rectal-wall infolding and descent of a separate small-bowel-containing sac. A draft calls both findings “rectal prolapse”. Explain how to make the description anatomically precise.
quiz.answer: Describe the rectal infolding as intussusception, stating how far it extends and whether it reaches or passes the anal canal. Separately describe the small-bowel-containing sac as an enterocele with its compartment and dynamic extent. Specify any external prolapse rather than using one broad term for different structures.
quiz.explain: Structural names should identify what moves and where it goes. This prevents two distinct mechanisms from being merged into an ambiguous label.

quiz.prompt: A follow-up report claims improved prolapse because the lowest measured position is smaller, but the patient barely strained. How would you reassess that comparison?
quiz.answer: Check the cine images and report reduced manoeuvre adequacy. Describe the positions actually observed, but qualify the apparent improvement because the functional challenge was weaker. Compare technique, reference line, landmarks and evacuation phase, and avoid declaring true anatomical improvement from noncomparable examinations.
quiz.explain: A measurement can be precise yet answer the wrong comparison. Functional effort is a confounder that must remain visible in the conclusion.

title: Breast Implants and the Male Breast
goal: Separate implant integrity from breast-parenchymal assessment, recognise rupture and implant-associated red flags, and distinguish typical gynaecomastia from a suspicious male breast lesion.

quiz.prompt: An MRI is requested solely for suspected silicone implant rupture. Which protocol choice answers that question?
choices: Routine dynamic contrast imaging alone
A dedicated non-contrast implant protocol with silicone-sensitive sequences
Only diffusion images
Only a thoracic spine localiser
quiz.answer: A dedicated non-contrast implant protocol with silicone-sensitive sequences
quiz.explain: Implant integrity depends on shell and silicone assessment. Contrast-enhanced breast imaging addresses a separate question, such as malignancy, and is added when indicated.

quiz.prompt: MRI demonstrates collapsed implant-shell lines within the fibrous capsule, without silicone outside that capsule. Which category fits?
choices: Extracapsular rupture
A definite implant-associated lymphoma
Intracapsular rupture
A malignant breast-parenchymal mass
quiz.answer: Intracapsular rupture
quiz.explain: The distinction depends on whether silicone extends beyond the fibrous capsule. Normal folds and other mimics require multiplanar review before diagnosing rupture.

quiz.prompt: Years after implantation, a patient develops a new unilateral peri-implant effusion. What should the interpretation prompt?
choices: Routine reassurance from fluid signal alone
Assume all late fluid represents mechanical rupture
Ignore the capsule if the implant shell appears intact
Targeted assessment for implant-associated disease, including tissue or fluid sampling when indicated
quiz.answer: Targeted assessment for implant-associated disease, including tissue or fluid sampling when indicated
quiz.explain: A delayed symptomatic collection merits evaluation of fluid, capsule, any mass and nodes. Imaging alone cannot diagnose or exclude implant-associated lymphoma.

quiz.prompt: A man has tender subareolar tissue with a fan-shaped pattern centred on the nipple. Which diagnosis is favoured?
choices: Gynaecomastia
A simple lipoma outside the breast
Invasive carcinoma in every case
A collapsed breast implant
quiz.answer: Gynaecomastia
quiz.explain: Typical gynaecomastia is centred behind the nipple. Correlate with examination, medications and symptoms rather than applying the female breast differential unchanged.

quiz.prompt: A man has an eccentric irregular solid breast mass and nipple retraction. What is the appropriate imaging conclusion?
choices: Male sex makes carcinoma implausible
A suspicious lesion requiring breast assessment and tissue diagnosis
Gynaecomastia regardless of morphology
A benign lesion unless bilateral
quiz.answer: A suspicious lesion requiring breast assessment and tissue diagnosis
quiz.explain: Eccentric location and malignant morphology are not explained by ordinary gynaecomastia. Use a diagnostic breast pathway and a clear assessment category.

quiz.prompt: An implant-integrity MRI shows no rupture. The referral also mentions a new palpable breast lump, but no dedicated parenchymal assessment was performed. Explain what the result does and does not establish.
quiz.answer: The result addresses implant integrity within the acquired protocol. It does not exclude a breast-parenchymal cause of the palpable lump. State that separate question explicitly and arrange or recommend the appropriate diagnostic breast assessment, with imaging targeted to the palpable site and clinical correlation.
quiz.explain: An implant and the surrounding breast are different targets. A normal answer to one should not be allowed to close the other.

quiz.prompt: Silicone-sensitive images show silicone beyond the implant capsule and in an axillary node. What anatomical details belong in the report before discussing management?
quiz.answer: Describe the side, implant type and position if known, shell appearance, and extracapsular silicone distribution. Localise affected breast or chest-wall tissues and the axillary finding, noting any associated mass or fluid. Separate evidence of silicone migration from assessment of unrelated suspicious breast findings.
quiz.explain: The distribution matters more than the rupture label alone. Mapping the findings allows the clinical team to connect symptoms, implant history and possible treatment.

quiz.prompt: A patient develops swelling years after implantation. Ultrasound shows a new effusion and an indeterminate capsular nodule. How would you communicate the concern without diagnosing lymphoma from imaging?
quiz.answer: Report the delayed effusion, nodule location and size, capsular findings and relevant nodes. State that implant-associated disease is a concern requiring specialist breast assessment and appropriate fluid or tissue evaluation. Imaging cannot determine whether the process is malignant, inflammatory or another cause on these findings alone.
quiz.explain: The concern should trigger the correct investigation while retaining diagnostic uncertainty. A named serious possibility is not the same as a confirmed diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: A man has typical subareolar glandular tissue, but examination identifies a separate hard lump lateral to the nipple. What error would occur if the report ended at gynaecomastia?
quiz.answer: It would leave the separate palpable abnormality unexplained. Correlate the exact lump location with targeted imaging, document whether a distinct lesion is present, and assess its morphology independently. Gynaecomastia can coexist with another lesion and should not be used to dismiss a discordant clinical finding.
quiz.explain: One correct diagnosis may be incomplete. Concordance requires explaining the finding that prompted the referral, not merely finding a benign abnormality nearby.

quiz.prompt: A male breast lesion is irregular and eccentric, but the draft recommends observation because male breast cancer is uncommon. Explain the reasoning error and improve the conclusion.
quiz.answer: Low background frequency does not make suspicious morphology benign. Describe the lesion and associated nipple, skin or nodal findings, assign the appropriate diagnostic assessment, and recommend tissue evaluation through the breast pathway. The conclusion should reflect this lesion's evidence rather than reassurance based only on sex.
quiz.explain: Population frequency informs prior probability. It does not override a concerning individual finding or remove the need for diagnostic concordance.

title: Imaging Pulsatile and Non-pulsatile Tinnitus
goal: Use pulsatility, otoscopy, hearing findings and neurological signs to choose targeted imaging and identify vascular, temporal-bone and retrocochlear causes.

quiz.prompt: Before choosing imaging for tinnitus, which clinical distinction most directly changes the search strategy?
choices: Whether the symptom follows the pulse
The scanner manufacturer
Whether the patient prefers CT
The length of the referral letter
quiz.answer: Whether the symptom follows the pulse
quiz.explain: Pulsatility directs attention toward vascular and related structural causes. Otoscopy, laterality, hearing findings and neurological symptoms further define the appropriate pathway.

quiz.prompt: Pulsatile tinnitus accompanies a retrotympanic lesion on otoscopy. Which study best depicts the bony temporal-bone anatomy and vascular canal relationships?
choices: Unenhanced lumbar MRI
Thin-section temporal-bone CT
A skull scout alone
Routine abdominal CT
quiz.answer: Thin-section temporal-bone CT
quiz.explain: High-resolution CT evaluates bone and canal anatomy. Additional vascular or contrast-enhanced imaging depends on the suspected lesion; an apparent middle-ear mass is not automatically inflammatory.

quiz.prompt: Unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus occurs with asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss. Which imaging target is especially relevant?
choices: The rectal wall
The rotator cuff
Internal auditory canals and cerebellopontine angles
The lumbar facet joints
quiz.answer: Internal auditory canals and cerebellopontine angles
quiz.explain: MRI can assess a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma. The audiological pattern and laterality determine the focused question.

quiz.prompt: Noninvasive imaging is unrevealing, but a specialist remains concerned about a dural arteriovenous fistula. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: A normal routine brain MRI excludes every fistula
No vascular assessment can add information
Tinnitus alone proves a fistula
Selected cases may need catheter angiography after specialist review
quiz.answer: Selected cases may need catheter angiography after specialist review
quiz.explain: Small shunts can evade a routine examination. Catheter angiography is an invasive problem-solving test when the residual clinical suspicion justifies it.

quiz.prompt: CT finds a jugular-bulb variant on the same side as tinnitus. How should causality be expressed?
choices: A potential correlate requiring clinical and anatomical correlation
A proven cause solely because it is ipsilateral
A finding that excludes all other causes
A malignant tumour unless biopsied
quiz.answer: A potential correlate requiring clinical and anatomical correlation
quiz.explain: Anatomical variants can be incidental. Report their relationship to the middle ear and bony covering, without converting coexistence into proof of symptom causation.

quiz.prompt: A tinnitus referral contains no information about pulsatility, side, hearing or otoscopy. Explain why ordering the same scan for every such referral is a poor protocol strategy.
quiz.answer: These details define different diagnostic targets. Clarify pulse synchrony, laterality, hearing findings, otoscopy and neurological symptoms. Pulsatile symptoms may require vascular or temporal-bone assessment, while selected unilateral non-pulsatile presentations raise a retrocochlear question. Choose the examination to answer the resulting clinical question rather than treating tinnitus as one anatomical diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Protocol selection begins with the phenotype of the symptom. Missing referral details can change both modality and anatomical coverage.

quiz.prompt: A routine non-contrast brain MRI is reported normal in a patient with persistent pulsatile tinnitus. The clinician asks whether that excludes a vascular shunt. How would you answer?
quiz.answer: No. State which vascular information the acquired study can and cannot provide. A normal routine brain examination is not equivalent to a negative dedicated vascular investigation. The need for further targeted imaging or catheter angiography depends on clinical suspicion, prior testing and specialist assessment.
quiz.explain: A test result must be interpreted against the protocol. Exclusion claims should not extend beyond its coverage and sensitivity.

quiz.prompt: A right jugular-bulb variant is found, but the patient describes left-sided tinnitus. How should this affect the impression?
quiz.answer: Record the variant and its relevant anatomical relationships, but note that its side does not match the reported symptom. Do not present it as the established cause. Confirm the clinical laterality and consider whether the actual symptomatic side and appropriate alternative causes have been adequately assessed.
quiz.explain: An attractive imaging finding can be incidental. Side concordance is a basic check against premature causal attribution.

quiz.prompt: Temporal-bone imaging shows a retrotympanic soft-tissue lesion adjacent to vascular structures. What should a useful report establish before a definitive lesion label is applied?
quiz.answer: Localise the lesion, describe its enhancement if assessed, bony changes and relationship to vascular canals and middle-ear structures. Consider a vascular lesion in the differential and identify any need for further characterisation. Avoid a definitive inflammatory or neoplastic label unsupported by the available imaging.
quiz.explain: Anatomical relationships can determine the next safe diagnostic step even when the precise histology remains uncertain.

quiz.prompt: An internal-auditory-canal MRI finds a small lesion during assessment of unilateral tinnitus. What information should the report provide beyond the lesion name?
quiz.answer: Record side, location within the canal or cerebellopontine angle, dimensions, enhancement and relevant nerve or brainstem relationships. Compare with prior imaging where available and describe study limitations. Relate the finding to the clinical side without implying that its size alone predicts hearing loss or symptom severity.
quiz.explain: An actionable report establishes a baseline and location. Imaging anatomy and clinical function remain related but distinct observations.

title: Trigeminal Neuralgia and Neuropathy
goal: Follow the trigeminal pathway from brainstem to peripheral branches, distinguish vascular contact from morphological compression, and search for secondary disease.

quiz.prompt: A vessel touches the cisternal trigeminal nerve but does not distort it. What should the report avoid?
choices: Naming the vessel
Describing the side
Calling contact alone definitive symptomatic neurovascular compression
Reviewing high-resolution multiplanar images
quiz.answer: Calling contact alone definitive symptomatic neurovascular compression
quiz.explain: Contact can occur without symptoms. A stronger imaging argument includes morphological nerve change at a relevant site, interpreted with the clinical side and syndrome.

quiz.prompt: A patient has progressive facial numbness rather than brief triggered pain. Where should the MRI search extend?
choices: Only the root entry zone
Only the cerebellar tonsils
Only the nasal cavity
The full pathway from brainstem through skull-base foramina and peripheral branches
quiz.answer: The full pathway from brainstem through skull-base foramina and peripheral branches
quiz.explain: Trigeminal neuropathy may arise at several anatomical levels. Full pathway assessment helps detect tumour, inflammation, demyelination and perineural spread.

quiz.prompt: An enhancing lesion occupies Meckel's cave and extends through a trigeminal skull-base foramen. Which reporting detail matters?
choices: The involved branch, foramen and proximal extension
Only the largest axial diameter
Only whether the ventricles are enlarged
The absence of a scalp lesion
quiz.answer: The involved branch, foramen and proximal extension
quiz.explain: Localise the lesion along the nerve and map foraminal and cavernous-sinus extension. This anatomy guides the differential and further evaluation.

quiz.prompt: A facial malignancy is followed by new V3 numbness. MRI shows thickening and enhancement along the mandibular nerve. What must be considered?
choices: A normal consequence of ageing
Perineural tumour spread
An isolated vestibular disorder
A diagnosis excluded by a small primary tumour
quiz.answer: Perineural tumour spread
quiz.explain: Symptoms and an abnormal nerve course raise concern for perineural spread. Trace the pathway to the foramen ovale and intracranial segments rather than stopping at the primary site.

quiz.prompt: A patient with facial sensory symptoms has a focal pontine T2 lesion near the trigeminal nuclei. Which principle applies?
choices: Every trigeminal symptom arises from an arterial loop
The brainstem can be excluded if the cisternal nerve looks normal
Central pathology can explain the symptom and needs its own differential
A pontine lesion proves metastatic disease
quiz.answer: Central pathology can explain the symptom and needs its own differential
quiz.explain: The pathway begins centrally. A pontine lesion requires assessment for demyelinating, vascular, neoplastic and inflammatory causes in the clinical context.

quiz.prompt: A vascular loop indents the left trigeminal nerve, but the patient's attacks are right-sided. How would you frame the finding and the remaining search?
quiz.answer: Describe the left-sided contact and morphological change accurately, but state the side mismatch. Do not attribute the right-sided symptoms to it without additional evidence. Review the right trigeminal pathway and consider alternative causes, with clinical confirmation of symptom side and distribution.
quiz.explain: Visible compression can be important without explaining the presenting syndrome. Anatomical and clinical concordance must be tested rather than assumed.

quiz.prompt: An MRI requested for facial numbness only includes thin cisternal sequences. Explain what it could miss and how the limitation should be reported.
quiz.answer: It may incompletely assess the brainstem, Meckel's cave, cavernous sinus, skull-base foramina and peripheral branches. State the actual coverage and avoid excluding disease throughout the trigeminal pathway. If symptoms suggest neuropathy or secondary disease, a broader targeted assessment may be needed.
quiz.explain: A focused sequence can answer a narrow question well while leaving other segments unevaluated. The report must preserve that boundary.

quiz.prompt: A treated facial tumour is followed by V2 numbness and enhancement extending toward the skull base. What distribution should the report trace rather than simply measuring the primary site?
quiz.answer: Trace the abnormality along the expected V2 pathway, including the pterygopalatine region, foramen rotundum and more proximal trigeminal structures as covered. Describe thickening, enhancement, foraminal change and intracranial extent, and state concern for perineural spread in the clinical context.
quiz.explain: Nerve-related spread follows an anatomical route that can extend beyond the apparent primary lesion. A route map can be more consequential than one tumour diameter.

quiz.prompt: The symptomatic trigeminal nerve is displaced by an adjacent lesion. A colleague reports “neurovascular conflict” without identifying a vessel. Explain how to correct the reasoning.
quiz.answer: First determine the nature of the adjacent structure using the available sequences and enhancement pattern. Describe the lesion, nerve displacement and location, and distinguish a mass-related effect from vascular contact. If the structure remains uncertain, report that uncertainty and the additional characterisation needed rather than assigning a mechanism by proximity alone.
quiz.explain: The mechanism requires identification of the responsible structure. Nerve displacement does not by itself establish a vascular cause.

quiz.prompt: The referral describes both brief triggered pain and progressive persistent numbness. Why should the imaging review not stop after finding an arterial contact?
quiz.answer: The arterial contact may be incidental or explain only part of the syndrome. Progressive sensory deficit warrants assessment of the full nerve pathway for secondary disease. Describe the contact, any morphological nerve change and any other abnormality, then correlate the imaging with both the pain pattern and persistent deficit.
quiz.explain: A single finding should not erase clinical features it fails to explain. The mixed presentation broadens the question being answered.

title: Sella and Parasellar MRI
goal: Localise sellar and parasellar lesions by epicentre, assess optic and cavernous-sinus relationships, recognise vascular mimics, and connect imaging with endocrine and visual findings.

quiz.prompt: A mass lies above the sella, and a normal pituitary gland is visible separately below it. Which first step improves the differential?
choices: Localise the epicentre before assuming a pituitary adenoma
Label every suprasellar mass an adenoma
Ignore the gland because the lesion is large
Classify the lesion only by its longest dimension
quiz.answer: Localise the epicentre before assuming a pituitary adenoma
quiz.explain: Identifying the normal gland and lesion epicentre narrows the possible tissue of origin. Signal and enhancement are interpreted after localisation.

quiz.prompt: A sellar mass extends superiorly in a patient with visual symptoms. Which relationship must be reported explicitly?
choices: Its distance from the frontal sinus only
Contact, displacement or compression of the optic apparatus
The number of visible scalp veins
The side of the nasal septal deviation
quiz.answer: Contact, displacement or compression of the optic apparatus
quiz.explain: Optic-apparatus involvement is clinically consequential. Describe its relationship to the lesion and integrate formal visual assessment rather than inferring visual function from MRI.

quiz.prompt: A parasellar lesion contains flow-related signal and is contiguous with the internal carotid artery. What should happen before tissue sampling is contemplated?
choices: Assume all enhancement represents meningioma
Ignore the vascular relationship
Evaluate for an aneurysm or other vascular lesion
Call it a cyst because it is rounded
quiz.answer: Evaluate for an aneurysm or other vascular lesion
quiz.explain: A vascular mimic must be recognised before intervention. Angiographic imaging can clarify vessel continuity and lumen; a rounded parasellar shape is not a tissue diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: Biochemistry suggests pituitary hypersecretion, but a routine thick-slice brain MRI is negative. Which study may better address the question?
choices: A chest radiograph
A lumbar CT
A repeat identical localiser
Dedicated thin-section pituitary MRI tailored to the endocrine question
quiz.answer: Dedicated thin-section pituitary MRI tailored to the endocrine question
quiz.explain: A small sellar lesion may be missed by a general brain protocol. Targeted imaging improves assessment, while interpretation still depends on the endocrine evidence.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a pituitary mass develops sudden severe headache and visual decline. MRI shows new intralesional haemorrhage. What is the reporting priority?
choices: Urgent communication of suspected pituitary apoplexy
Routine annual comparison only
Assuming haemorrhage proves malignant transformation
Waiting for lesion growth before reporting the change
quiz.answer: Urgent communication of suspected pituitary apoplexy
quiz.explain: The acute syndrome can threaten vision and endocrine function. Communicate the finding promptly and describe optic-apparatus compression and relevant extension.

quiz.prompt: A rounded suprasellar lesion is found, but the pituitary gland is not identified separately on a routine brain study. Explain how you would organise the differential and the next imaging question.
quiz.answer: First establish the epicentre and relationship to the gland, stalk, optic apparatus, cavernous sinuses and vessels. Describe cystic, solid, haemorrhagic or flow-related features without assuming pituitary origin. A dedicated sellar study or vascular assessment may be needed to resolve the uncertain origin and anatomy.
quiz.explain: Localisation constrains the differential. Naming a familiar sellar lesion before finding the normal structures risks anchoring on the wrong tissue of origin.

quiz.prompt: A pituitary lesion is visible in a patient with abnormal hormone tests. The draft calls it “definitely hormone-secreting” based only on enhancement. Explain the limitation.
quiz.answer: MRI describes the lesion's presence, size and anatomical effects but does not establish its secretory behaviour from enhancement alone. Correlate with the specific endocrine findings and relevant clinical assessment. Report whether the imaging and laboratory question are anatomically compatible without replacing biochemical diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Morphology and hormonal function are different types of evidence. A plausible relationship still needs clinical confirmation.

quiz.prompt: A sellar mass contacts the optic chiasm without obvious compression. The patient reports worsening vision. What should the report communicate?
quiz.answer: State the contact and any displacement or signal abnormality that is actually visible, and preserve the distinction between contact and compression. Highlight the visual symptoms as requiring prompt clinical and formal visual assessment. The absence of dramatic compression on MRI does not establish normal visual function.
quiz.explain: The image cannot substitute for examination of the patient's vision. Anatomical precision and clinical urgency should both remain clear.

quiz.prompt: A parasellar mass has an apparent connection to the carotid artery, but slow flow or thrombus makes the appearance unclear. What is the key unresolved issue before proposing a biopsy?
quiz.answer: A vascular lesion, including an aneurysm, must be assessed before tissue sampling is proposed. Describe the suspected arterial continuity and uncertain components, and obtain appropriate vascular characterisation through the clinical team. Do not use a solid-appearing or partially thrombosed component to exclude a vascular origin.
quiz.explain: The consequence of mistaking a vascular lesion for a tissue mass makes the anatomical uncertainty decisive for planning.

quiz.prompt: A follow-up scan shows haemorrhage within a known pituitary mass. The requisition mentions a sudden severe headache and new visual loss. Explain why a routine “interval signal change” conclusion is inadequate.
quiz.answer: The acute symptoms and haemorrhage raise concern for pituitary apoplexy. State and urgently communicate that concern, describe the optic-apparatus relationship and extension, and record communication. The clinical team must assess visual and endocrine consequences rather than treating the finding as an incidental change on surveillance.
quiz.explain: The same imaging change has different importance in an acute syndrome. The report should connect the finding to the time-sensitive clinical presentation.

title: Elbow MRI: Tendons, Ligaments and Nerves
goal: Read the elbow by anatomical compartments, link ligament and tendon injury to mechanics, distinguish normal pseudodefects, and describe nerve and osteochondral abnormalities.
articles: Ulnar collateral ligament of elbow joint

quiz.prompt: A coronal elbow image suggests a capitellar defect, but sagittal images localise it to the posterior non-articular surface. Which possibility should be considered?
choices: Normal capitellar pseudodefect
A definite unstable osteochondral fragment
An acute fracture in every patient
A displaced radial-head fragment
quiz.answer: Normal capitellar pseudodefect
quiz.explain: Correlating planes prevents a normal contour from becoming a false osteochondral diagnosis. Examine the articular surface and associated marrow or cartilage abnormality.

quiz.prompt: A throwing athlete has medial elbow pain under valgus stress. Which structure needs directed assessment?
choices: The deltoid ligament
The ulnar collateral ligament
The anterior talofibular ligament
The scapholunate ligament
quiz.answer: The ulnar collateral ligament
quiz.explain: The medial ligament complex resists valgus load. Describe the involved portion, attachment, fibre continuity and accompanying flexor-pronator or osteochondral findings.

quiz.prompt: There is sudden antecubital pain and loss of supination strength. MRI shows a retracted tendon proximal to the radial tuberosity. Which tendon is involved?
choices: Triceps tendon
Common extensor tendon
Distal biceps tendon
Patellar tendon
quiz.answer: Distal biceps tendon
quiz.explain: The distal biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity. Report tear completeness, retraction and associated anatomy that may matter to repair planning.

quiz.prompt: MRI shows common extensor-origin tendinosis in a patient with lateral pain. What additional structure should be reviewed for associated instability?
choices: The Achilles tendon
The plantar plate
The medial meniscus
The lateral collateral ligament complex
quiz.answer: The lateral collateral ligament complex
quiz.explain: Adjacent tendon and ligament abnormalities may coexist. A tendon finding should not end the search when the clinical question includes instability.

quiz.prompt: Persistent elbow pain is accompanied by ulnar-distribution paraesthesia. Which assessment complements the joint review?
choices: Ulnar nerve calibre, signal, course and potential compression
Only the radiocapitellar cartilage
Only the humeral marrow
Only a count of loose bodies
quiz.answer: Ulnar nerve calibre, signal, course and potential compression
quiz.explain: A nerve-related symptom needs a targeted nerve assessment. Ultrasound and MRI provide complementary structural information; clinical examination and electrodiagnostic findings may also be relevant.

quiz.prompt: A suspected capitellar defect appears on one coronal slice. Sagittal images show it at the posterior non-articular margin, with no convincing adjacent abnormality. Explain how you would avoid overcalling an osteochondral injury.
quiz.answer: Correlate the location and contour across planes and consider a normal capitellar pseudodefect. Review the true articular surface, cartilage, marrow and any loose fragment or other injury. If the appearance is a normal variant, describe it accordingly rather than assigning pathology from one slice.
quiz.explain: Single-plane appearances can be misleading. Anatomical localisation provides a stronger check than the visual drama of the initial image.

quiz.prompt: MRI suggests a distal biceps tear, but the report contains only the word “rupture”. What additional observations would make the report useful to the treating team?
quiz.answer: Describe whether the tear is partial or complete, its insertional location, the amount and direction of retraction, and tendon quality as assessable. Include surrounding fluid or other injury and any limitation in identifying the tendon ends. These observations provide the anatomical basis for clinical planning.
quiz.explain: A tear label does not express the geometry or extent of injury. The report should show where the relevant structures now lie.

quiz.prompt: A throwing athlete has medial pain and an abnormal ulnar collateral ligament on MRI. Why should review include the surrounding joint and tendons?
quiz.answer: The clinical load pattern can affect more than one structure. Describe the ligament abnormality and its attachment, then assess the flexor-pronator origin, articular surfaces, marrow and other associated findings. Correlate with symptoms and instability rather than assuming the first abnormality accounts for the whole presentation.
quiz.explain: Mechanical syndromes can produce a constellation of findings. A complete compartmental review avoids reducing the examination to a single structure.

quiz.prompt: A patient has ulnar-distribution paraesthesia, but the elbow MRI report discusses only cartilage and tendons. Identify the missing interpretive task and its limits.
quiz.answer: Review the ulnar nerve along the covered course for calibre, signal and structural causes of compression, and describe relevant surrounding anatomy. A structurally normal MRI does not exclude every functional neuropathy. Correlate with examination and, when indicated, electrodiagnostic or dynamic ultrasound assessment.
quiz.explain: The symptom determines an additional target. Structural imaging and functional nerve assessment contribute different information.

quiz.prompt: Motion degrades the sequence intended to show a collateral ligament. Other images show adjacent oedema but not the fibres clearly. How should tear severity be reported?
quiz.answer: Describe the oedema and suspected injury, but state that fibre continuity and tear severity cannot be confidently assessed because of motion. Avoid assigning a complete rupture solely from surrounding signal change. Explain which clinical question remains unresolved and whether additional targeted assessment would change management.
quiz.explain: Secondary signs can support suspicion without establishing structural completeness. The certainty of the grade must match the direct evidence.

title: Neonatal Spine Ultrasound
goal: Perform an age-appropriate spinal ultrasound, document vertebral numbering and conus position, assess filum and root motion, and recognise dysraphism and study limitations.

quiz.prompt: A young infant is referred with an atypical sacral skin marker. Why can ultrasound depict the spinal canal particularly well at this age?
choices: The posterior elements are incompletely ossified
The spinal cord is outside the canal
Ultrasound penetrates fully ossified adult bone equally well
The infant has no cauda equina
quiz.answer: The posterior elements are incompletely ossified
quiz.explain: The immature posterior elements provide an acoustic window. The window becomes more limited with ossification, so age and image quality affect confidence.

quiz.prompt: The conus seems low, but the lumbosacral junction is uncertain. What should be resolved before assigning a vertebral level?
choices: The ultrasound machine brand
Vertebral numbering and the landmark used to count
Only the infant's weight
Only the skin-marker colour
quiz.answer: Vertebral numbering and the landmark used to count
quiz.explain: An incorrect count can produce a false low-conus diagnosis. Document the numbering method and use correlation or further imaging when the landmarks remain uncertain.

quiz.prompt: Only a midline sagittal still image has been saved. What important part of a neonatal spinal examination is missing?
choices: A routine oral contrast study
A chest radiograph in every infant
Transverse assessment and evaluation of cord or root movement
An obligatory contrast-enhanced sequence
quiz.answer: Transverse assessment and evaluation of cord or root movement
quiz.explain: Multiple planes and dynamic assessment add information about filum, roots and canal contents. A single still image cannot represent the complete examination.

quiz.prompt: Ultrasound suggests an abnormal filum and limited root motion, but the acoustic window is poor. What is the appropriate conclusion?
choices: Definite normality because ultrasound has no radiation
Tethering is excluded without further assessment
A precise operative recommendation from the incomplete study
State suspicion and limitations, with further specialist-directed evaluation
quiz.answer: State suspicion and limitations, with further specialist-directed evaluation
quiz.explain: The report should distinguish a concerning observation from a complete anatomical diagnosis. MRI can characterise suspected dysraphism when ultrasound is abnormal or incomplete.

quiz.prompt: An infant has an exposed open spinal lesion. Which safety principle applies?
choices: Do not place a routine ultrasound probe directly on the exposed lesion
Compress the lesion to improve resolution
Apply nonsterile gel to confirm the defect
Delay clinical referral until after repeated compression views
quiz.answer: Do not place a routine ultrasound probe directly on the exposed lesion
quiz.explain: Direct scanning of an open defect risks contamination and adds little to the obvious lesion. Follow the specialist pathway and appropriate infection precautions.

quiz.prompt: A neonatal ultrasound labels the conus “L3” after counting from an uncertain sacral landmark. The conclusion says tethered cord. Explain the steps needed before accepting that conclusion.
quiz.answer: Confirm vertebral numbering using reliable landmarks and document the method, age and any segmentation uncertainty. Reassess conus position alongside the filum, cord and root movement and associated abnormalities. If ultrasound remains indeterminate or concerning, further specialist-directed imaging is needed; an uncertain number alone should not establish tethering.
quiz.explain: A precise-looking vertebral label can conceal an uncertain count. The diagnosis requires concordant anatomy rather than a solitary unsupported level.

quiz.prompt: Only sagittal still images were recorded in an infant with an atypical skin marker. The conus looks normal on one image. Explain why this does not document a complete normal examination.
quiz.answer: The study lacks transverse and dynamic documentation needed to assess canal contents, filum and root movement adequately. State what is visible and what has not been evaluated, including vertebral numbering and the relationship to the skin marker. Completion or further evaluation depends on the clinical question and technical window.
quiz.explain: A normal-looking structure in one projection does not establish normality of the whole examination. Documentation should support each conclusion.

quiz.prompt: An older infant has a limited ultrasound acoustic window, with the distal cord poorly seen. The referral is for suspected dysraphism. Write an appropriate conclusion and next-step rationale.
quiz.answer: The distal cord and relevant canal anatomy are incompletely assessed because of the limited window, so dysraphism is not excluded. Describe any observed abnormalities and recommend specialist-directed further assessment, commonly MRI when detailed anatomy is required. The limitation, rather than a presumed normal result, determines what remains to be answered.
quiz.explain: Ultrasound's usefulness depends on the window. A modality without radiation can still be nondiagnostic for the specific patient and question.

quiz.prompt: A small cystic focus near the distal cord is seen, but conus position, filum and nerve-root motion are otherwise reassuring. How would you avoid turning an isolated observation into an unsupported diagnosis?
quiz.answer: Localise and describe the cystic focus, assess its relationship to the cord and filum, and evaluate for associated abnormalities. Consider a recognised developmental variant in the appropriate context, but state any uncertainty. Do not diagnose clinically significant dysraphism or tethering from a small isolated cystic appearance alone.
quiz.explain: The significance of a focal finding depends on its location and accompanying anatomy. Pattern assessment protects against both dismissal and overdiagnosis.

quiz.prompt: An infant with an exposed spinal defect is sent for “ultrasound confirmation”. Explain how you would handle the request without applying a routine probe directly to the lesion.
quiz.answer: Clarify the question with the neonatal or specialist team and avoid direct routine scanning of the open defect because of contamination risk and limited added value. Follow the clinical pathway and infection precautions. If another covered region or associated finding requires ultrasound, define that separate question and appropriate technique.
quiz.explain: The requested test should add information safely. An already visible open abnormality does not justify a routine examination across exposed tissue.

title: Bowel Ultrasound: Technique and Normal Anatomy
goal: Optimise bowel ultrasound for depth and resolution, use graded compression and anatomical landmarks, assess the wall and mesentery, and state which segments were not visualised.

quiz.prompt: A superficial ileal loop is poorly resolved with a low-frequency curved probe. Which adjustment is most useful?
choices: Increase image smoothing until the layers disappear
Use a higher-frequency linear probe if penetration remains adequate
Measure only the gas interface
Assume superficial bowel cannot be examined
quiz.answer: Use a higher-frequency linear probe if penetration remains adequate
quiz.explain: Probe frequency balances resolution against penetration. Select it for the depth of the target after compression, and optimise focus and gain before measurement.

quiz.prompt: Gas obscures a bowel segment. What is the purpose of controlled graded compression?
choices: To guarantee exclusion of perforation
To replace the need for another imaging modality in every case
To displace intervening gas and assess compressibility
To create a fixed normal wall-thickness value
quiz.answer: To displace intervening gas and assess compressibility
quiz.explain: Compression improves access to some loops and supplies dynamic information. It should be controlled and tolerable; persistent nonvisualisation is a limitation, not a normal finding.

quiz.prompt: A short segment appears thickened on one oblique image. What should be checked before calling disease?
choices: Only the colour of the transducer
Whether the saved image has a label
Whether the patient has eaten this week
Perpendicular wall measurement, distension, layering and adjacent findings
quiz.answer: Perpendicular wall measurement, distension, layering and adjacent findings
quiz.explain: Obliquity and contraction can simulate thickening. Assess the segment in more than one plane and integrate mural stratification, vascularity and surrounding tissues.

quiz.prompt: The appendix has not been identified despite a careful study. Which report statement is most accurate?
choices: Appendix not visualised; document secondary signs and study limitations
Normal appendix definitively demonstrated
Appendicitis excluded in all circumstances
The caecum must therefore be absent
quiz.answer: Appendix not visualised; document secondary signs and study limitations
quiz.explain: Nonvisualisation and demonstrated normality are different results. The clinical probability and secondary signs determine whether observation or further evaluation is needed.

quiz.prompt: A bowel-ultrasound report lists wall thickness alone. Which addition most improves its diagnostic value?
choices: Only the room number
Length and distribution, layering, Doppler signal, motility and extramural findings
Only the examination start time
Only the nominal probe frequency
quiz.answer: Length and distribution, layering, Doppler signal, motility and extramural findings
quiz.explain: Bowel disease has a spatial and dynamic pattern. A reproducible segmental report includes the lumen, wall and surrounding mesentery, with acquisition limitations stated.

quiz.prompt: A measured bowel wall is 5 mm on an oblique image and thinner when measured perpendicular to the wall. Explain which measurement should be trusted and what else belongs in the assessment.
quiz.answer: Use a reproducible perpendicular measurement on an adequately visualised segment, with its degree of distension and compression considered. Assess length, distribution, layering, Doppler signal and surrounding tissues. Do not infer disease from an oblique measurement that may exaggerate thickness or from a single numeric threshold in isolation.
quiz.explain: Geometry and acquisition affect measurement. A number should be interpreted within a documented segmental pattern.

quiz.prompt: A follow-up intestinal ultrasound reports improvement because Doppler signal is lower, but the gain and flow settings differ. How would you reassess the claim?
quiz.answer: Check whether settings, depth, compression and sampling conditions were comparable. Describe the observed signal but qualify the apparent change if technical differences could explain it. Correlate with wall morphology, extent and other findings rather than using an unstandardised Doppler comparison as sole evidence of improvement.
quiz.explain: Doppler appearance is partly a measurement of the acquisition. Longitudinal claims require comparable technique as well as biological plausibility.

quiz.prompt: The symptomatic right lower quadrant is examined, but neither appendix nor terminal ileum is confidently seen. No collection is identified. Write a conclusion that does not overstate the negative study.
quiz.answer: The appendix and terminal ileum were not confidently visualised. No collection was demonstrated within the assessed region, but the study does not exclude pathology in the unvisualised structures. Document limiting factors and any secondary signs, and relate further evaluation to the ongoing clinical probability and symptoms.
quiz.explain: Absence of a collection answers a narrower question than exclusion of appendiceal or ileal disease. The conclusion should retain that distinction.

quiz.prompt: A short bowel segment appears abnormal, but adjacent fat and lymph nodes have not been assessed. Why should the operator expand the examination beyond the bowel wall?
quiz.answer: Extramural tissues can help characterise the process and reveal complications or alternative causes. Assess mesenteric fat, nodes, collections, free fluid and relevant vessels, while documenting the segment and extent. Interpret these findings with mural layering, motility and vascularity rather than treating wall thickness as a standalone diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Bowel disease has relationships outside the lumen. A complete local survey can change both the differential and the urgency.

quiz.prompt: A superficial bowel loop is sharply depicted with a linear probe, but deeper loops are not adequately penetrated. What should an appropriate scanning and reporting strategy do?
quiz.answer: Use a suitable lower-frequency probe or adjusted settings to survey deeper targets, while retaining the higher-frequency assessment for accessible detail. Record which regions remain limited. Do not generalise a well-seen superficial segment into a normal examination of the whole bowel.
quiz.explain: The best probe for one depth may be inadequate for another. Coverage and detail are complementary requirements.

title: Craniosynostosis and Skull Shape
goal: Relate skull shape to suture anatomy, distinguish positional deformity from suspected synostosis, select proportionate imaging and describe single- or multisuture involvement.

quiz.prompt: Clinical examination shows a typical positional plagiocephaly without concerning features. What is the usual imaging principle?
choices: Routine CT is mandatory for every asymmetrical head
Clinical assessment is often sufficient; reserve imaging for uncertainty
MRI under anaesthesia is always first line
A skull radiograph proves normal brain development
quiz.answer: Clinical assessment is often sufficient; reserve imaging for uncertainty
quiz.explain: Typical positional deformity can usually be diagnosed clinically. Imaging is used when the diagnosis is uncertain or synostosis is suspected, with radiation considered in modality selection.

quiz.prompt: An infant has a long narrow skull, and sagittal-suture fusion is suspected. Which shape term fits?
choices: Trigonocephaly
Unilateral anterior plagiocephaly
Scaphocephaly
Hydrocephalus
quiz.answer: Scaphocephaly
quiz.explain: Sagittal fusion restricts transverse growth and produces an elongated skull pattern. Confirm the suture finding in the clinical context rather than using shape alone as proof.

quiz.prompt: A closed metopic suture is seen in an infant with no triangular forehead or orbital deformity. What should the report avoid?
choices: Recording the skull shape
Considering the infant's age
Reviewing the other sutures
Diagnosing pathological trigonocephaly from closure alone
quiz.answer: Diagnosing pathological trigonocephaly from closure alone
quiz.explain: Metopic closure may be physiological. The associated frontal and orbital morphology separates an isolated ridge from a clinically significant synostotic shape.

quiz.prompt: Clinical assessment cannot distinguish positional flattening from a fused suture, and local paediatric ultrasound expertise is available. What is a reasonable first targeted test?
choices: Ultrasound of the suspected suture
Routine multiphase contrast CT
Lumbar MRI
A bone scan of the whole skeleton
quiz.answer: Ultrasound of the suspected suture
quiz.explain: Suture ultrasound can resolve an equivocal examination without ionising radiation. Further imaging depends on confidence, specialist assessment and the need for operative planning.

quiz.prompt: CT confirms several fused sutures with an unusual skull shape. What reporting approach is most useful?
choices: Name only the most obvious suture
List each involved suture and associated craniofacial or intracranial findings
Assume every case is isolated
Describe only the cosmetic appearance
quiz.answer: List each involved suture and associated craniofacial or intracranial findings
quiz.explain: Multisuture disease requires an anatomical map and assessment for complications or associated abnormalities. Clear distribution supports craniofacial-team evaluation.

quiz.prompt: A family requests CT for an infant whose clinical assessment confidently shows typical positional plagiocephaly. Explain a proportionate imaging response.
quiz.answer: Explain that a confident clinical diagnosis often does not require imaging. Clarify whether there are features suggesting synostosis or another unresolved question; if not, a CT is unlikely to add necessary diagnostic information. If uncertainty exists, targeted assessment and appropriate lower-radiation or nonionising options can be considered with the specialist team.
quiz.explain: Imaging should answer a remaining question. Reassurance does not require an examination that adds little to an already secure clinical assessment.

quiz.prompt: Suture ultrasound is reassuring over one segment, but part of the suspected suture cannot be assessed. The infant has a progressive abnormal skull shape. How should the conclusion be qualified?
quiz.answer: State which suture segments were shown and which remain unassessed. A normal visible segment does not exclude partial fusion elsewhere. The progressive clinical shape keeps the question open, so specialist assessment and further imaging may be required if the uncertainty will affect diagnosis or planning.
quiz.explain: The sampled anatomy bounds the exclusion. Combining an incomplete negative test with persistent clinical concern is more accurate than declaring the whole suture open.

quiz.prompt: An infant has a palpable metopic ridge and an apparently closed metopic suture. Why should the report also describe forehead and orbital shape?
quiz.answer: Metopic closure or a ridge can occur without pathological trigonocephaly. Describe the frontal contour, symmetry and orbital configuration, with age and clinical examination considered. The overall morphology determines whether the suture appearance is part of a concerning deformity rather than making closure alone the diagnosis.
quiz.explain: A developmental feature gains significance from its anatomical context. The report should avoid converting one finding into a complete syndrome.

quiz.prompt: A scan obtained for suspected single-suture disease shows fusion involving more than one suture. What should the report add beyond correcting the initial diagnosis?
quiz.answer: List each involved suture and the resulting cranial asymmetry or shape, describe relevant craniofacial and intracranial findings within coverage, and note complications or limitations. Communicate the multisuture pattern to the craniofacial team because it changes the anatomical assessment and may prompt evaluation for associated disease.
quiz.explain: The referral hypothesis should not constrain the final search. A map of all affected sutures provides a better basis for specialist review.

quiz.prompt: A low-dose CT clearly depicts fused sutures but has limited soft-tissue detail. The report states “normal brain and no associated abnormalities”. Explain how to correct this overreach.
quiz.answer: Retain the confident suture and bony findings, but describe the limitations of the low-dose examination for intracranial soft tissues. Report only abnormalities or normal relationships that are adequately assessed. If there is a specific concern about brain structures or complications, identify it as a separate question requiring suitable evaluation.
quiz.explain: Optimising an examination for bone can limit other conclusions. The strength of the suture assessment does not transfer automatically to the brain.
